newsitem.title: GERMANY: Nestle may use gene soybeans - magazine.
newsitem.headline: Nestle may use gene soybeans - magazine.

text.p: Swiss food giant Nestle SA said it will use genetically altered soybeans in its food products, even though its German subsidiary had said it would not.
Nestle will speed up the introduction of the new ingredients to find out how consumers "really react," chairman Helmut Maucher told the German weekly news magazine Stern.
An October 25 statement by the company's German subsidiary was "not useful without the addition that we generally have a positive attitude to biotechnology," said Maucher.

Nestle Deutschland AG said at the time it would not use soy products derived from the new U.S. crop in response to expected consumer opposition, as campaigners were citing possible health risks from the genetically altered soybeans, developed by Monsanto Co, mixed in with ordinary beans.
This would only apply to Nestle's German operations which used just 2,000 tonnes of soybeans per year.

Anti-gene soya protestors have used consumer polls which they say are negative to back up a wave of demonstrations at soya processors and food companies, demanding a boycott of the products or at least clear labelling.
On Monday, environmentalist group Greenpeace staged a protest against the products at Nestle headquarters in Vevey in Switzerland.
Maucher said the heated debate in Germany would not stop genetically altered foods.
Labelling also only offered limited solutions because many products contained too many raw materials, making proof of existing traces of genetically altered organisms impossible.

Neslte would use raw materials derived from the new beans in its "Maggi" product range of instant soups, in breakfast cereals and possibly in baby food, but it would use extreme caution in this sensitive area, Maucher said.
Nestle Deutschland in Frankfurt was not immediately available for comment on whether the chairman's comments overruled the German statement.
